Lessons.Title: Solving Problems with Inequalities in Two Variables
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: match a two-variable inequality to its graphical solution region and relevant ordered pairs, use graphing technology when available and interpret solutions under contextual restrictions. Original Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U02:L23, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/23/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). The source explicitly asks for graphing technology and matching equation, graph, point and description. Graph generation must be observed rather than inferred from written output.

Independent context: a community stall uses two materials, A at $3 per unit and B at $5 per unit, with at most $60 for supplies. Let a,b≥0 be whole-number units. The inequality is 3a+5b≤60. The boundary has intercepts (20,0),(0,12) and should be solid; the feasible region is the first-quadrant portion at or below the line. Do not include negative quantities despite the larger mathematical half-plane.

Point (5,9) has cost $60, so it is on and included. Point (7,8) costs $61, so it is outside. Point (10,6) costs $60 and also belongs to the boundary; point (0,0) is inside. A graphing system must be given the actual inequality and an appropriate window; if unavailable, produce a clearly labelled manual graph, not an invented software screenshot.

Student activity: match at least two independently made graph windows, an inequality, a verbal budget interpretation and a candidate point; use graphing technology to verify region and line inclusion where actually available. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correct model, boundaries and shading, point/classification checks, and authentic or explicitly simulated graphing explanation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Graph window
KeyConcepts.Definition: A plotting range must show meaningful intercepts and feasible region.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Select axes covering a≥0,b≥0 and intercepts.
KeyConcepts.Example: Line intercepts (20,0) and (0,12) fit within a 0–22 by 0–14 window.

KeyConcepts.Title: Budget half-plane
KeyConcepts.Definition: A linear budget inequality includes all affordable combinations.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Graph equality boundary then shade the side that passes a test point.

KeyConcepts.Title: Context and integer solutions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A continuous half-plane may contain points impossible in a discrete purchase.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Require nonnegative whole numbers of units.
KeyConcepts.Example: (5,9) is a valid integer budget plan.

WorkedExamples.Title: Graph the budget constraint
WorkedExamples.Question: Describe the region 3a+5b≤60.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the stated inequality system, use valid domains and independently verify each numerical case.
Steps: Set b=0 to obtain a=20; set a=0 to obtain b=12.
Test origin cost 0≤60 and shade below the solid boundary.
Restrict to whole a,b≥0 in context.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify valid and invalid points
WorkedExamples.Question: Are (5,9) and (7,8) feasible?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the stated inequality system, use valid domains and independently verify each numerical case.
Steps: Budget includes equality, so this pair is feasible.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish graphing from physical domain
WorkedExamples.Question: Would (−5,15) solve the cost inequality?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the stated inequality system, use valid domains and independently verify each numerical case.
Steps: Thus the pair is on the full mathematical boundary.
But a negative count of material A is impossible.
It fails the extra contextual domain a≥0.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both the budget and count-domain checks are necessary.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming a graphing-calculator plot proves actual purchase feasibility
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Negative or noninteger coordinates may satisfy the numerical inequality.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Omitting the boundary because of a misread sign

SummaryPoints: Graphing technology visualizes half-planes but requires an appropriate view window.
3a+5b≤60 uses a solid line with intercepts (20,0),(0,12).
Physical constraints can exclude mathematical solution points.
Teacher judges graph interpretation and actual software use.
